name: Behentrimonium chloride

lead: Behentrimonium chloride is the waxy conditioning ingredient in many hair conditioners. It is what makes wet hair feel slippery and easy to detangle, and what leaves dry hair with less static and a smoother, sleeker look.

It works through charge: its positively charged head is attracted to the negatively charged surface of hair, while its long 22-carbon fatty tail forms a lubricating layer on the strand. It is used as part of a whole conditioner formula rather than on its own, and published research on its hair effects specifically is limited.

paras: People get it simply by using a conditioner that lists it, applied after shampooing and rinsed out. It is usually combined with fatty alcohols and oils in the same formula, and the smoother feel shows up as soon as the hair is dry.

At the levels used in rinse-off products it is described as acceptable, but in concentrated form it irritates skin and eyes. It is very toxic to aquatic life. Anyone who reacts to conditioners containing it can check ingredient lists for it.

angle.text: Behentrimonium chloride is the conditioning agent that makes hair slippery, easier to detangle and less static, so it looks smoother and sleeker after washing. It clings to the hair surface and lubricates the strand, and you get the effect through the conditioner it is formulated in.

lead: Behentrimonium chloride (also docosyltrimethylammonium chloride, BTAC-228) is a quaternary ammonium compound that acts as a cationic surfactant. It is a yellow, waxlike solid with the formula C25H54ClN [1][2]. Listed on conditioner labels, it is one of the ingredients that makes hair feel slippery and detangled in the shower and smoother, softer and less frizzy once dry, which is how it contributes to looking well-groomed.

It is used in cosmetics, chiefly hair conditioners, as an antistatic and conditioning agent; its positively charged head group binds to negatively charged hair surfaces, and its long fatty chain is described as smoothing the hair and reducing static [1][2][3]. Wikipedia lists uses in conditioners, hair dyes, mousses and some detergents [1].

A 2026 laboratory study that compared four cationic surfactants on human hair reported that longer-chain surfactants such as behentrimonium chloride showed superior deposition and conditioning, and that it outperformed the related behentrimonium methosulfate [3]. A post-marketing safety assessment of leave-on lotions containing it also exists [4].
infobox: Cetrimonium chloride and bromide; behentrimonium methosulfate [1][3]

paras: The molecule consists of a 22-carbon chain derived from behenic acid attached to a trimethylammonium group, with a chloride counter-ion; its IUPAC name is N,N,N-trimethyldocosan-1-aminium chloride [1][2]. It has a molar mass of about 404 g/mol [1][2]. The compound is described as poorly soluble in cold water and soluble in hot water [2], and Grokipedia reports a melting range of 60 to 90 degrees C, depending on purity [2].

Grokipedia reports that the C22 raw material is typically obtained from behenic acid in colza (rapeseed) oil, converted to the tertiary amine and quaternized with methyl chloride; that source is AI-generated and was used only as background [2]. Cetrimonium chloride and bromide are shorter-chain analogues [1].

Hair surfaces carry a net negative charge, especially when damaged. Streaming-potential (electrokinetic) studies show that cationic conditioning agents adsorb onto hair through electrostatic attraction, and that molecular weight and charge density determine how thick the deposited layer is [5]. In a comparison of four cationic surfactants, behentrimonium chloride, with its long chain, showed stronger deposition and conditioning than shorter-chain or bulkier-headed surfactants, a result the authors attributed to stronger van der Waals interactions; its chloride counter-ion was suggested to explain its edge over the methosulfate form [3]. Wet-combing measurements and spectroscopy were used in that work to evaluate conditioning [3].

Wikipedia lists uses as an antistatic agent, a disinfectant in some applications, and an ingredient in conditioners, hair dyes, mousses and detergents [1]. Grokipedia describes its role in conditioners as helping to smooth the cuticle and improve manageability, and notes limited use in skin care and fabric softeners [2]. It is commonly paired with fatty alcohols such as cetyl or behenyl alcohol in conditioner bases.

A paper on its safety notes it is a straight-chain alkyltrimonium chloride used as an antistatic, hair conditioning, emulsifier or preservative agent in personal care products, and that the European Union restricted alkyltrimonium chlorides and bromides as preservatives to 0.1 percent or less, while they have been used for many years at up to 5 percent for other purposes [4].

Grokipedia reports that it is considered acceptable in rinse-off products at concentrations up to 4% when formulated to avoid irritation, may irritate skin and eyes at higher concentrations, and is classed as very toxic to aquatic life [2]. In a 2013 study, leave-on skin care products with 1 to 5 percent behentrimonium chloride were predicted to be non-irritants in EpiDerm skin and bovine corneal ocular tests, showed no allergic contact dermatitis or cumulative irritation in human occlusive patch tests, and produced no clinically assessed or self-reported adverse reactions in adults or children with atopic, eczematous or dry skin over two to four weeks of home use [4]. Wikipedia notes laboratory tests indicating ready biodegradability, and Grokipedia reports more than 60 percent degradation in 28 days for category members [1][2].

No studies found of hair-appearance outcomes for behentrimonium chloride in people. Related research includes an in vitro, clinical and post-marketing safety assessment of leave-on lotions containing 1 to 5 percent of the compound [4] and laboratory electrokinetic studies on human hair [5][3].
